question: What is Netflix's theatrical window policy as of the 3Q26 call?
expected: Traditional 45-day window for a handful of films (e.g. Narnia), not all films as Sally Barton's note says.

result.answer:
Netflix does not have a single standard window [2, 7]. On the 3Q26 call, Ted Sarandos said Netflix is "a streaming first business" [1]. He also said the roughly 30 theatrical releases this year, about the same as last year, each have their own "bespoke release pattern" [2].

- **Specialty releases:** Another specialty release, "mosquito ball" in the transcript, is described as "a bit shorter" [4].
- **Big family films:** These get a 45-day window and a wide theatrical release [5]. Sarandos named Greta Gerwig's Narnia and the animated feature Charlie versus the Chocolate Factory [5].
- **David Fincher film (Cliff Booth):** Not confirmed in the cited documents.
- **Overall:** Sarandos said the strategy now includes "a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films." Netflix is also now reporting box office grosses for these releases [7].

**Correction to an analyst note:** Sally Barton's note says Netflix is moving to a "standard 45-day theatrical window for all of its films" [8]. The transcript does not support this [2, 7]. The 45-day window applies to a handful of films, and specialty releases get a 47-day window or a shorter one [3][4][7].

citations.passage: But a reminder, we are a streaming first business.
And yes, we're going to release about 30 films theatrically this year, pretty much what we did last year. And each 1 of these have their own kind of bespoke release pattern.
So for specialty releases, we're doing a 47-day window platform theatrical release for La Boulange right now.
And then we also upcoming have a theatrical release for mosquito ball, a bit shorter.

Now for those big family movies I talked about, we've already announced we have a 45-day window and a wide theatrical release for Greta Gerwig's new movie, Narnia, the Magician's Nephew. And for our animated feature Charlie versus the Chocolate Factory.
And in that one, we've done a deal with IMAX to put them on the biggest screens for a couple of weeks, 4 weeks before the Netflix release.

It's involved to include a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films -- but the other 1 that's been important to folks is that we are also now reporting box office grosses for those releases when we do it.

result.answer: Netflix has not given a numerical 2027 revenue growth guide [1, 2]. question: What Azure growth did Microsoft guide to for FY27 Q2, and what did it say the guide depends on?
expected: 49-50% cc; depends on finding more efficiency gains beyond Q1's, plus token pricing / capacity uncertainty.

result.answer:
Microsoft guided FY27 Q2 (Oct–Dec 2026) Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency [1, 3, 7]. Q1 growth was 48% [1][2].

What Amy Hood said the guide depends on:
- Continued efficiency gains across the CPU and GPU fleet [1]. These help offset some third-party (3P) GPU-as-a-service contracts that were delayed to H2 [1].
- Finding more efficiency gains [3, 6]. In Q&A she said the Q1 gains continue into Q2, but "We need to find some more, which we're counting on" to reach the guide [3].
- Supply she had counted on for Q2 that moved out into H2 [3]. She said the efficiency work also has to help cover that [3].
- Token pricing [3, 4]. She said there is "some unknown on some token pricing through the quarter," and that "That stuff can change." [3] She also said token pricing was higher than expected in Q1 [4].
- Customer demand still exceeds available supply, so supply is the constraint [1].

Beyond Q2, she said year-over-year growth will keep reflecting the timing and scale of engineering efficiencies, new capacity adds, and a strong prior-year comparison [5].

Sally Barton's note makes the same point, which matches the transcript [3, 6]. She says the guide depends on more efficiency gains and uncertain token pricing, and her view is that this makes it "less mechanical than usual" [6]. That last phrase is her opinion [6]. Joe Smith's note gives the same 49–50% figure [7].

citations.passage: In Azure, we expect revenue growth of 49 to 50% in constant currency with continued efficiency gains across our CPU and GPU fleet helping to offset some 3P GPU as a service contracts that have been delayed to H2. Customer demand continues to exceed available supply.
Azure revenue was ahead of expectations and increased 48%, even with the 3P capacity delays noted earlier, driven by Foundry and improved CPU monetization.

We need to find some more, which we’re counting on, enable to get to that guidance that I gave because I have faith in the teams who work in Q1 continuing into Q2. But we also need that work to be able to help us a little bit because we had some supply we were counting on Q2 move out into H2. And so, I think, and to your point, there’s also some unknown on some token pricing through the quarter. That stuff can change.
We had higher token pricing than we expected in the quarter.

And looking beyond Q2, year-over-year growth will continue to reflect the timing and scale of engineering efficiencies delivered in the quarter, and new capacity adds, as well as a strong prior-year comparable that included accelerating growth in the second half.

question: How did JPMorgan's full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance change between the 1Q26 and 2Q26 calls, and why?
expected: ~$95B (held on 1Q) raised to ~$96.5B on 2Q, driven mainly by deposit balances rather than rates.

result.answer:
JPMorgan raised its full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance by $1.5B, from about $95B to about $96.5B [1, 2].

**1Q26 call:** Barnum said "we continue to expect NII ex [1]. Markets to be about $95 billion." [1] Total NII was cut to about $103B because Markets NII fell to about $8B. [1]

**2Q26 call:** Management "now expect[s] NII ex [2]. Markets to be about $96.5 billion." Total NII is about $105.5B, with Markets NII rising to about $9B. [2]

**Why it rose (Barnum, Q&A):**
- **Deposit balances were the biggest factor.** He cited balances across both Wholesale and Consumer, including a mix shift toward slightly higher-margin deposits. [3]
- **Rates were a little higher.** Rates were somewhat higher than at the last guidance, at both the short end and the back end. [3]
- **Consumer betas helped.** He said actual sensitivity is probably a bit more than the EaR suggests, because consumer betas outperformed the model. [4]
- **Overall split.** "A little bit of the increase" came from higher rates, but "most of it is balances overall." [5]
- **Exit run rate.** He said the math suggests a higher exit run rate [6]. This is in the central case, which assumes the yield curve follows the forwards and deposits and other drivers match current expectations. [6]

**Markets NII shift:** Barnum said equity allocated to the CIB increased, which moves some equity, and a little NII, from Corporate into the CIB. [7] He said this NII moves out of NII ex-Markets into Markets NII. [7] He put that piece at probably about $150M, and said it is part of the increase not expected to be offset in the bottom line. [8]

**Analyst notes:** Joe Smith's and Sally Barton's 2Q26 notes both give the $96.5B figure and attribute the rise mostly to deposit balances [9, 10]. This matches the transcript. [9][10] Sally Barton's note also says card NCO guidance "went up to ~3.6%". [11] The transcript says management now expects a Card net charge-off rate of about 3.2%, so that part of her note is wrong. [12] This doesn't affect the NII answer.

citations.passage: In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we continue to expect NII ex. Markets to be about $95 billion. We now expect total NII to be approximately $103 billion, as a function of Markets NII decreasing to about $8 billion, predominantly due to rates, which we expect will be primarily offset in NIR.

In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we now expect NII ex. Markets to be about $96.5 billion and total NII to be approximately $105.5 billion as a function of Markets NII increasing to about $9 billion.

Just mechanically in terms of the drivers of the upward revision, the biggest single factor is deposit balances, I would say, across both Wholesale and Consumer, both sort of the overall quantum of it, but also like mix shift inside of that in favor of slightly higher margin overall. And then, rates are like a little bit higher than when we previously guided both in the short-end and in the back-end.

And probably our actual sensitivity is a little bit more than the EaR suggests right now because of the outperformance of the consumer betas relative to the model, and that difference is probably disproportionately in the front-end.
So, when you assemble that together, you have a little bit of the increase as a function of higher rates, but most of it is balances overall.

And if you sort of do that math, it does suggest a higher exit run rate, which in the central case, assuming the yield curve plays out as the forwards currently forecast and the deposit and other drivers are in line with our current expectations, that's what we would expect.

And the consequence of that is to move some equity essentially out of Corporate into the CIB, and a lot of that is Markets. That obviously comes with a little bit of NII. And so, that NII is moving out of NII ex. into Markets NII.
This piece, which to be fair is quite small, it's probably like $150 million, is a part of the increase that we would not expect to be offset in the bottom line, all else equal.

question: How did Azure growth in FY27 Q1 compare with what Microsoft guided on the FY26 Q4 call?

result.answer:
Azure grew 48% in FY27 Q1, which was 3 points above the roughly 45% constant-currency growth Microsoft guided on the FY26 Q4 call [1, 2].

- Guidance (FY26 Q4 call): CFO Amy Hood said, "In Azure, we expect revenue growth of approximately 45% in constant currency." [1]
- Actual (FY27 Q1): she said Azure was ahead of expectations and increased 48%, even with delayed third-party capacity, driven by Foundry and improved CPU monetization. [2] The excerpt doesn't say whether the 48% is reported or constant currency.
- Reasons for the beat: Hood cited GPU fleet efficiency gains that let Microsoft allocate more capacity to customers, and higher revenue per token [3]. She also said CPU engineering work identified and monetized underutilized capacity. [3]
- Next quarter: Microsoft guided FY27 Q2 Azure growth to 49-50% in constant currency. [4]

Errors in analyst notes:
- Joe Smith's FY26 Q4 note says Azure grew 48% in that quarter. [5] The transcript says 43%. [6] The 48% figure is the FY27 Q1 result.
- Joe Smith's FY27 Q1 note says commercial bookings "grew 12%." [7] The transcript says they decreased 12%. [8] This doesn't affect the Azure comparison.

Joe Smith's FY27 Q1 note matches the transcript on the 48% result and the 49-50% Q2 guide. [9] Sally Barton's FY27 Q1 note states the same Q2 guide. [10] The Barton note also says Azure "accelerated to 48%," which is consistent with the transcript.

Foundry revenue more than tripled year-over-year with upside driven by efficiency gains across our GPU fleet that allowed us to allocate additional capacity to customers, as well as higher revenue per token that we benefited from in the quarter. Across our CPU fleet, engineering work enabled us to identify and monetize underutilized capacity this quarter, helping us serve more of the growing demand with our existing capacity.

In Azure, we expect revenue growth of 49 to 50% in constant currency with continued efficiency gains across our CPU and GPU fleet helping to offset some 3P GPU as a service contracts that have been delayed to H2.

question: Did JPMorgan raise its full-year 2026 expense guidance on the 1Q26 call?
expected: No - held at ~$105B (Joe Smith's note wrongly says raised to ~$107B). It was raised to ~$107.5B on the 2Q26 call.

result.answer:
No [1, 3]. On the 1Q26 call JPMorgan held its full-year 2026 adjusted expense outlook at about $105 billion [1]. CFO Jeremy Barnum said it "continues to be about $105 billion" [1]. Asked about it in Q&A, he said you might otherwise have expected the company to revise up the full-year expense guidance [2]. On the failure to revise, he said it was "just a little early in the year" and to see how things play out over the next quarter or so [3].
